concept.name: CAP Theorem & Consistency Models
concept.tagline: Reason about consistency, availability, and partition tolerance—and choose linearizable, sequential, or eventual models deliberately.

spark.summary: During a network partition, a distributed store cannot simultaneously provide both strong consistency and full availability; engineering chooses which guarantee to weaken and how clients observe stale reads.
spark.keyTakeaway: Name the partition behavior first, then pick a consistency model and client contract that matches product risk—not the buzzword on the slide.

concept.whyItMatters: Misunderstanding CAP leads to silent data loss, double spends, and “always available” APIs that lie during splits.
whenToUse: Caches in front of authoritative stores
whenNotToUse: Single-node databases with no partition risk
Batch analytics with no online SLA
keyPoints: CP vs AP is a partition-time trade-off

examples.title: Banking ledger during partition
examples.scenario: Two regions lose connectivity during a transfer spike.
examples.outcome: CP design may reject writes; AP design may expose divergent balances until merge.

tradeOffs.con: Higher latency and availability hits during partitions

failureModes.name: Split-brain writes
failureModes.mitigation: Fencing tokens, epoch numbers, or quorum leases.

deepDive.markdownContent:
## CAP under partitions

Consistency and availability tensions appear only when messages between nodes are lost or delayed.

caseStudy.solution: Chose CP quorum writes with explicit unavailable responses
